title: Time & Work
summary: Rates, LCM units and the men-days chain solve nearly every question: combined work, efficiency ratios, pipes and cisterns, mid-work join/leave, alternate days, provisions and wages. One slot is near-guaranteed in Tier 1, with staged pipe problems and wage splits rising in Tier 2.

subtopics.title: Work Rates & the LCM Method
subtopics.concept:
Think of a whole job as 1 unit. A person who finishes in T days works at rate $\frac{1}{T}$ per day.

$$\text{combined rate} = \frac{1}{T_1} + \frac{1}{T_2} + \cdots, \qquad T_{\text{together}} = \frac{1}{\text{combined rate}}$$

**LCM method (no fractions):** take total work = LCM of the given days. If A takes 12 and B takes 24, set work = 24 units; A does 2/day, B does 1/day; together 3/day ⇒ 8 days. Whole numbers only — faster and safer.

**Symmetry shortcut:** two workers of times a and b together take $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ days.

tricks.title: LCM units, not fractions
tricks.body: Set the job to the LCM of the individual times; rates become small integers.

tricks.body: For exactly two workers, one formula — no addition of fractions.

mistakes: Adding the days ($12 + 24 = 36$) instead of adding the rates.
For three workers, applying $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ pairwise instead of the three-way formula.
Forgetting the combined time must be less than the smallest individual time.
Mixing units — one rate in days, another in hours.
subtopics.notes:
### Work, time and rate
In these questions "work" means one whole job — building a wall, filling a tank, stitching shirts. The **rate** of a worker is the part of the job he finishes in one day (or one hour). If A finishes the whole job in T days, his rate is $\frac{1}{T}$ of the job per day. Two rules run the whole topic:

$$\text{Work done} = \text{rate} \times \text{time}, \qquad \text{rates add when people work together}$$

When two people work together, their rates simply add — each does his own bit every day. So the combined time is always **less than the fastest individual time**. If your answer is bigger, you added days instead of rates.

### The LCM method — whole numbers, no fractions
Fractions slow you down and cause sign slips. Instead, give the job a size in **units**: take the LCM of all the individual times.
A finishes in 15 days, B in 10 days. Let the job = 30 units (LCM of 15 and 10). A does $30 \div 15 = 2$ units a day, B does 3 units a day. Together $5$ units a day → $30 \div 5 = 6$ days. Every number here is a small whole number — that is the whole point of the method.

### Combining two workers
For exactly two workers with times a and b:
$$T = \frac{ab}{a + b}$$
Example: 6 and 12 days → $\frac{6 \times 12}{18} = 4$ days. This is the same as the LCM method — try it once to convince yourself, then use whichever is faster.
The reverse question is just as common: "A and B together take 6 days, A alone takes 10 — find B alone." Subtract the rates: $\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{15}$ → 15 days.

### Three or more workers
Add all three rates. A, B, C take 9, 12, 18 days: job = 36 units, rates $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ a day → 4 days. As a formula, three workers take
$$T = \frac{abc}{ab + bc + ca}$$

### Pairwise data (A+B, B+C, A+C)
When the three pair-times are given, add the three pair-rates — each person's rate now appears **twice** — and halve:
$$\frac{1}{T_{AB}} + \frac{1}{T_{BC}} + \frac{1}{T_{AC}} = 2\left(\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B} + \frac{1}{T_C}\right)$$
Pairs take 10, 12 and 15 days: sum of pair rates $= \frac{15}{60} = \frac14$ → trio rate $\frac18$ → all three together take 8 days. To find one person alone, subtract a pair from the trio: A = trio − (B+C).

### Partial work statements
"A can do $\frac{3}{5}$ of a work in 12 days." Scale to the whole job: full time $= 12 \times \frac{5}{3} = 20$ days. Convert every worker to a full-work time first, then combine as usual. With the LCM method this is equally quick: if the job is 35 units and A does 21 units in 12 days, his rate is $\frac{21}{12} = \frac74$ units a day.

### Common traps
- Adding the individual days (15 + 10 = 25) instead of the rates.
- In "together minus one" questions, subtracting the times instead of the rates.
- Partial work: scaling the days by the given fraction instead of its reciprocal.
- Forgetting the sanity check — a combined time must beat the best single time.

### Quick revision
- Rate = 1/time; rates add; Work = rate × time.
- Two workers: $T = \frac{ab}{a+b}$. Three: $T = \frac{abc}{ab+bc+ca}$.
- Together − A = B: subtract rates, never days.
- Pairwise times: add the three pair-rates, halve → trio rate.
- Partial work: full time = days × (reciprocal of fraction).

patterns.name: Two workers together (or the reverse)
patterns.howToSpot: Two individual completion times are given and the time together is asked — or the together time and one person's time are given and the other person's time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Take the job as LCM units, or write each rate as $\frac{1}{T}$.
2. Together: add the rates, then time = work ÷ combined rate.
3. Reverse: subtract one rate from the together rate to get the missing worker.

Why: each worker carries his own share of work every day, so rates add (or subtract).

example.q: A finishes a job in 15 days and B in 10 days. Working together, in how many days do they finish it?

patterns.name: Three or more workers together
patterns.howToSpot: Three individual times are given (or two times plus the trio time) and the combined time — or one missing individual time — is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Job = LCM of the given times; find each rate in units per day.
2. Add the rates; divide the job by the total rate.
3. To find a missing rate, subtract the known rates from the trio rate.

Why: the whole job is split among the workers, so the daily shares add up to the trio's share.

example.q: A, B and C can do a piece of work in 9, 12 and 18 days respectively. In how many days will they finish it together?
example.solution: Job = 36 units; rates $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ a day → $36 \div 9 = 4$ days.

patterns.name: Pairwise combination times
patterns.howToSpot: 'A and B together take …, B and C together take …, A and C together take …' — the trio time or one person's time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert the three pair-times to pair-rates.
2. Add all three: each worker's rate is counted twice, so halve the sum for the trio rate.
3. Any individual's rate = trio rate − the pair-rate not containing him.

Why: in the sum of the three pair-rates, A appears in two pairs, and so do B and C.

example.q: A and B can do a work in 10 days, B and C in 12 days, A and C in 15 days. In how many days will all three finish it together?

patterns.name: Fractional / partial work statements
patterns.howToSpot: 'A can do 3/5 of the work in 12 days', 'B does 2/7 of the work in 8 days' — the full-work time, or the together time, is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Scale each statement to the whole job: full time = days given × reciprocal of the fraction.
2. Combine the full-work times like any other question.
3. In LCM units, the rate is simply (units done) ÷ (days taken).

Why: a worker's rate is fixed, so completing only a fraction just means he worked on a smaller job for the given days.

example.q: A can do $\frac{5}{6}$ of a work in 10 days and B can do $\frac{3}{8}$ of the same work in 9 days. Working together, in how many days will they complete the work?
example.solution:
A's full time $= 10 \times \frac65 = 12$ days; B's $= 9 \times \frac83 = 24$ days.
Together: $\frac1{12}+\frac1{24} = \frac18$ → 8 days.

subtopics.title: Efficiency, 'Twice as Good' & Ratio Cases
subtopics.concept:
Efficiency is rate. **Efficiency is inversely proportional to time**: twice as efficient ⇒ half the days.

$$\frac{\text{efficiency}_A}{\text{efficiency}_B} = \frac{\text{time}_B}{\text{time}_A}$$

If A is k times as good as B and together they take T days: rate $= (k+1)$ units ⇒ B alone takes $(k+1)T$ days, A alone takes $\frac{(k+1)T}{k}$ days.

Convert every 'twice as good / half as efficient' statement into a rate ratio first — everything else is arithmetic.

tricks.title: Rate units from the efficiency ratio
tricks.body: Let B = 1 unit/day, A = k units/day; total = (k+1)/day.

example.q: A is twice as efficient as B, and together they finish a job in 12 days. B alone would take:
example.solution: Units: A + B = 3/day = whole job in 12 ⇒ job = 36 units ⇒ B alone = **36 days** (A: 18).

tricks.title: Invert, never scale
tricks.body: 'A is 3 times as good' ⇒ A's days = B's days ÷ 3.

example.q: A is 3 times as efficient as B and together they complete the work in 12 days. A alone takes:

tricks.title: Days-difference cases
tricks.body: 'B takes 24 days more than A' plus an efficiency ratio pins both times.

example.q: A is 3 times as fast as B and takes 24 days less than B. Together they would finish the work in:
example.solution: Times x and 3x with 3x − x = 24 ⇒ x = 12, so A = 12, B = 36; together $\frac{36}{4} = 9$ days.

mistakes: Scaling days when told efficiency scales ('twice as good' means HALF the days, not double).
Adding efficiencies as days.
Using $kT$ for the stronger worker's time instead of $\frac{(k+1)T}{k}$.
Ignoring that 'x times as fast' and 'x% more efficient' set up different ratios.
subtopics.notes:
### Efficiency is rate with a comparison
"Efficient" here does not mean clever — it means **works faster**. Efficiency is another name for rate. The one relation to remember:

$$\frac{\text{efficiency of A}}{\text{efficiency of B}} = \frac{\text{time of B}}{\text{time of A}}$$

Efficiency and time are **inversely proportional**: twice as efficient → half the days. Three times as efficient → one-third of the days. Write every statement as a rate ratio before doing anything else.

### The unit trick for "k times as good"
If A is k times as efficient as B, let B do 1 unit a day and A do k units a day. Together $(k+1)$ units a day. If together they take T days, the whole job is $(k+1)T$ units, so:
$$\text{B alone} = (k+1)T \text{ days}, \qquad \text{A alone} = \frac{(k+1)T}{k} \text{ days}$$
A is twice as efficient as B; together 18 days → job $= 3 \times 18 = 54$ units → B alone 54 days, A alone 27. Notice B (the weaker worker) takes the longer time — if you assign 54 to A, you inverted the ratio.

### Efficiency given as a ratio
"A and B work in the ratio 3 : 2" — same idea. Rates $3u$ and $2u$; together $5u$. If the together time is 15 days, the job is $75u$, so B alone takes $\frac{75u}{2u} = 37.5$ days. If B's own time is given instead, first get u from it.

### "50% more efficient" and friends
Percentages become ratios at sight: 50% more efficient → ratio $3 : 2$; 25% more efficient → $5 : 4$; 20% less efficient → $4 : 5$. Then continue exactly as above. A is 50% more efficient than B and B takes 27 days → A's rate $= \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{1}{27} = \frac{1}{18}$; together $\frac{1}{18} + \frac{1}{27} = \frac{5}{54}$ → $10.8$ days.

### Days-difference questions
"A is twice as fast as B and finishes 12 days earlier." Times are $x$ and $2x$, and $2x - x = 12$, so A = 12, B = 24; together $\frac{12 \times 24}{36} = 8$ days. With ratio $a : b$ for A : B efficiency, times are in $b : a$ — set the difference equal to the given gap and everything falls out.

### Why the inverse rule never fails
Rate × time = 1 whole job (constant). If the rate is multiplied by k, the time must be divided by k for the product to stay 1. That is all "inversely proportional" means, and it is why scaling days in the wrong direction gives an impossible answer — the strongest worker always takes the fewest days.

### Common traps
- Reading "twice as efficient" as "twice the days" — efficiency and time move opposite ways.
- Giving the k-times worker $(k+1)T$ instead of $\frac{(k+1)T}{k}$ — that belongs to the weaker worker.
- Treating "25% more efficient" as a ratio of 25 : 100; it is 125 : 100 = 5 : 4.
- Mixing up whose time is longer in days-difference questions.

### Quick revision
- Efficiency ratio = rate ratio = inverse time ratio.
- k-times worker, together T days: weaker $(k+1)T$, stronger $\frac{(k+1)T}{k}$.
- 50% / 25% / 20% more efficient → 3:2 / 5:4 / 6:5.
- Days gap with times $bx$ and $ax$: $(b-a)x =$ gap.
- Sanity check: faster worker → fewer days, always.

patterns.name: 'k times as efficient', together time given
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is twice/thrice as efficient as B and together they finish in T days' — the individual times are asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Let the weaker worker do 1 unit/day, the stronger k units/day.
2. Together $(k+1)$ units/day → whole job $= (k+1) \times T$ units.
3. Divide by each worker's own rate to get his days.

Why: the together time prices the job in units; each worker then spends those units at his own speed.

example.q: A is twice as efficient as B and together they complete a work in 18 days. B alone can complete it in:
example.solution: Job $= (2+1) \times 18 = 54$ units → B alone 54 days (A alone 27 days).

patterns.name: Efficiency ratio given as a : b
patterns.howToSpot: An explicit ratio like 3 : 2 or 4 : 5 is given for the efficiencies, with either the together time or one person's time.
patterns.logic:
1. Fix rates $au$ and $bu$ per day.
2. From the given time, price the job in units.
3. Divide the job by the rate whose time is asked.

Why: a ratio is only a k-times statement written for both workers at once.

example.q: The efficiencies of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 2. B alone can finish the work in 30 days. Working together, they will finish it in:

patterns.name: Efficiency ratio plus a gap of days
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is twice as fast as B and takes 12 days less' — find either individual time or the together time.
patterns.formula: b x - a x = \text{gap}, \text{ where times are } bx \text{ and } ax
patterns.logic:
1. With efficiency ratio $a:b$, the times are in $b:a$ — call them $bx$ and $ax$.
2. Put the difference equal to the given gap and solve for x.
3. Now combine the two times with $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ if the together time is asked.

Why: the gap is a difference of two numbers in a known ratio, so one bracket pins both.

example.q: A is twice as fast a worker as B and takes 12 days less than B to finish a piece of work. Working together, they will finish it in:
example.solution:
Times $x$ and $2x$: $2x - x = 12$ → A 12 days, B 24 days.
Together $= \frac{12 \times 24}{36} = 8$ days.

patterns.name: Percent more / less efficient
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is 50% more efficient than B', 'A works 20% faster' — percentages of efficiency instead of a ratio.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert to a ratio: 50% more → 3 : 2; 25% more → 5 : 4; 20% less → 4 : 5.
2. Continue with the unit method (price the job, then divide).

Why: "a% more efficient" means rate $= \left(1 + \frac{a}{100}\right) \times$ the other's rate.

subtopics.title: Pipes & Cisterns
subtopics.concept:
Inlets fill (+rate), outlets/leaks drain (−rate). Treat the tank as 1 unit (or LCM litres).

$$\text{net rate} = \sum_{\text{inlets}} \frac{1}{T_i} - \sum_{\text{outlets}} \frac{1}{T_j}, \qquad \text{time} = \frac{1}{\text{net rate}}$$

**Two pipes, one filling one emptying:** net time $= \frac{ab}{b - a}$ (a = fill time, b > a = empty time).

Stage-based problems: compute the work already done in the first stage, then re-solve the remainder with the new set of pipes.

tricks.title: Sign discipline
tricks.body: Empty pipes subtract. Write + and − before adding anything.

example.q: Two pipes fill a tank in 8 hours and 12 hours; a third empties it in 6 hours. With all three open, the tank fills in:

tricks.title: Stage the problem
tricks.body: Finish stage 1 first, then treat the remainder as a fresh tank.

example.q: Pipes A (12 h) and B (16 h) fill a tank. Both run for 4 hours, then a drain (24 h) is also opened. The tank is full after how many more hours?
example.solution: In 4 h: $\frac{7}{48} \times 4 = \frac{7}{12}$ done. New rate $= \frac{7}{48} - \frac{1}{24} = \frac{5}{48}$, so the remainder takes $\frac{5}{12} \div \frac{5}{48} = 4$ h ⇒ total **8 hours**.

tricks.title: Fill-and-drain pair formula
tricks.body: One inlet, one outlet: net time = ab/(b − a).

example.q: A pipe fills a tank in 10 hours; a leak empties the full tank in 15 hours. With both, the tank fills in:

mistakes: Adding an outlet's rate instead of subtracting it.
Forgetting the tank may already be part-full when a new pipe opens.
Using $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ for a fill-drain pair (that formula is for two inlets).
Reporting the stage-1 time instead of the total time.
subtopics.notes:
### Pipes are workers with signs
A pipe that fills a tank is an **inlet**; its rate is positive. A pipe (or a leak) that empties the tank is an **outlet**; its rate is negative. Measure the tank in LCM units — litres or just "units" — exactly as in work problems.
A fills in 12 hours → $+1$ tank per 12 h. B empties in 24 hours → $-\frac{1}{24}$ per hour. Everything else is bookkeeping:
$$\text{net rate} = (\text{sum of inlet rates}) - (\text{sum of outlet rates}), \qquad \text{time} = \frac{\text{tank}}{\text{net rate}}$$

### One inlet, one outlet
A fills in a hours, B empties in b hours ($b > a$). Net rate $= \frac1a - \frac1b$, so the tank fills in
$$T = \frac{ab}{b - a}$$
10 and 15 → $\frac{150}{5} = 30$ hours. Note the minus sign in the denominator — the two-inlet formula $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ is a different question.

### More than one of each
Add every inlet rate, subtract every outlet rate. 8 h and 12 h filling, 24 h emptying: take the tank as 24 units → $3 + 2 - 1 = 4$ units/h → 6 hours. Watch the sign of the net rate: if the outlets win, the tank never fills (some questions ask exactly this — the answer is "it will never fill").

### Staged problems (pipes opened or closed mid-way)
Work stage by stage:
1. Compute the work done in stage 1 = (stage-1 rate) × (stage-1 time).
2. Find what fraction of the tank is still empty.
3. Re-solve the remainder as a fresh, smaller tank with the new set of pipes.
A (10 h) and B (15 h) run 2 hours: 30-unit tank, rate 5 → 10 units done, 20 left. A drain C (30 h) now opens: net $5 - 1 = 4$ units/h → 5 hours more, 7 hours total. Always read carefully whether the question wants the **extra** time or the **total** time — both are asked.

### The reverse leak question
"A tank fills in 8 hours normally, but a leak at the bottom makes it take 8 hours 40 minutes. How long would the leak take to empty a full tank?" Treat the leak as an unknown outlet: its rate = normal fill rate − slow fill rate $= \frac18 - \frac{3}{26} = \frac{1}{104}$ → the leak empties the full tank in 104 hours.

### The empty tank with a leak from the start
Tank full, leak alone empties it in x hours, inlet alone fills the empty tank in y hours — with both acting from empty, fill time $= \frac{xy}{x - y}$ (same fill–drain formula; the leak must be slower than the inlet for filling to be possible at all).

### Common traps
- Adding an outlet's rate instead of subtracting it.
- Using $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ (two-inlets formula) for a fill–drain pair.
- Reporting the stage-1 time or the stage-2 time when the total was asked.
- Forgetting the tank may already be part-full when the new pipe opens.

### Quick revision
- Inlets +, outlets −; net rate = inlets − outlets.
- Fill–drain pair: $T = \frac{ab}{b-a}$.
- Stage it: work done in stage 1, then a fresh smaller tank.
- Reverse leak: leak rate = fast rate − slow rate; leak time = reciprocal.
- Net rate ≤ 0 → the tank never fills.

patterns.name: Two or three inlets together
patterns.howToSpot: Two or three pipes all filling the same tank, individual fill times given, combined fill time asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Tank = LCM of the fill times; rates in units/hour.
2. Add the rates; time = tank ÷ total rate.
3. Two inlets only: use $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ directly.

Why: every pipe pours its own share each hour, exactly like workers on a job.

example.q: Two pipes can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. With both open together, the tank is filled in:

patterns.name: Inlets and outlets together (net rate)
patterns.howToSpot: Filling pipes and an emptying pipe (or leak) are open at the same time; the fill time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Mark each pipe + (fills) or − (empties) before any arithmetic.
2. Tank in LCM units; add inlets, subtract outlets.
3. Time = tank ÷ net rate. A fill–drain pair alone is $\frac{ab}{b-a}$.

Why: an outlet undoes work, so it must cancel part of the inlets' contribution.

example.q: Two pipes fill a tank in 8 hours and 12 hours, while a third pipe empties it in 24 hours. With all three open, the tank fills in:

patterns.name: Reverse: find the leak / outlet from two fill times
patterns.howToSpot: 'The tank fills in t hours normally but takes t′ hours because of a leak' — the leak's solo emptying time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Fast fill rate $= \frac1t$, slow (with leak) $= \frac{1}{t'}$.
2. Leak rate $=$ fast − slow; invert for the leak's own emptying time.
3. Put t′ in the same units as t (40 minutes = $\frac23$ hour).

Why: the only difference between the two runs is the leak, so the rate gap belongs to the leak alone.

example.q: A cistern normally fills in 8 hours, but a leak at the bottom makes it take 8 hours 40 minutes. The leak alone can empty the full cistern in:
example.solution: Slow time $= \frac{26}{3}$ h. Leak rate $= \frac18 - \frac{3}{26} = \frac{13-12}{104} = \frac{1}{104}$ → 104 hours.

patterns.name: Staged pipes — opened or closed mid-way
patterns.howToSpot: Pipes run for a few hours, then another pipe opens (or one closes); the remaining or total time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Stage 1: work done = rate × time; find the empty part left.
2. Stage 2: recompute the net rate with the new set of pipes.
3. Divide the remainder by the stage-2 rate; add stage times if the total is asked.

Why: the tank remembers only how much water is in it — stages are independent rate problems.

example.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours. Both run for 2 hours; then a drain pipe C, which can empty the full tank in 30 hours, is also opened. The total time to fill the tank is:
example.solution:
Tank = 30 units; stage 1: $5 \times 2 = 10$ done, 20 left.
Stage 2: $5 - 1 = 4$ units/h → 5 h more → total **7 hours**.

subtopics.title: Men–Days–Hours Chain & Provisions
subtopics.concept:
Work is the product of every resource: $\text{Work} = M \times D \times H \times E$ (men, days, hours/day, efficiency).

$$\frac{M_1 D_1 H_1 E_1}{W_1} = \frac{M_2 D_2 H_2 E_2}{W_2}$$

**Same work ⇒ equal products:** $M_1 D_1 = M_2 D_2$. More men ⇒ fewer days (inverse proportion).

**Provisions problems:** stock = men × days. After t days, remaining stock feeds the new headcount: $\text{days} = \frac{M_1 D_{\text{left}}}{M_2}$.

Consumption questions (garrison, fodder, food stores) are men-days problems in disguise.

tricks.title: Multiply resources, equate products
tricks.body: Everything inverse-proportional lands in the numerator; direct-proportional in the denominator.

example.q: 15 men complete a work in 20 days. In how many days will 25 men complete the same work?

tricks.title: Provisions after reinforcement
tricks.body: Stock left = original men × days left; then divide by the new headcount.

example.q: A garrison of 500 men has provisions for 27 days. After 3 days, 300 more men join. The provisions will now last:

tricks.title: Work left after a share is done
tricks.body: First find what fraction remains, then apply men-days to that remainder.

example.q: 45 men start a job they would finish in 16 days. After 4 days, 36 more men join. The remaining work now takes:

mistakes: Putting more men in the numerator of the chain equation (more men ⇒ fewer days ⇒ denominator).
Forgetting to subtract elapsed days in provisions problems.
Counting efficiency twice — E belongs inside the product once.
Applying men-days to the whole work instead of the remaining work.
subtopics.notes:
### Work as a product of resources
The same job can be finished by many men in few days or few men in many days. The bridge between the two situations is that the **total work stays the same**, and total work is the product of every resource:
$$\text{Work} = M \times D \times H \times E$$
(men × days × hours per day × efficiency). Equating the products of two situations:
$$\frac{M_1 D_1 H_1 E_1}{W_1} = \frac{M_2 D_2 H_2 E_2}{W_2}$$
For the same work, drop the W's. Quantities that grow with days (men, hours, efficiency) sit beside M; write the missing quantity last and solve. 18 men × 25 days = 450 man-days; with 30 men, $\frac{450}{30} = 15$ days. More men → fewer days: men and days are inversely proportional.

### Hours per day in the chain
12 men working 8 hours a day finish in 15 days: work $= 12 \times 15 \times 8 = 1440$ man-hours. How long for 18 men at 10 hours a day? $\frac{1440}{18 \times 10} = 8$ days. Hours behave exactly like days — more hours a day, fewer days needed.

### Provisions (garrison, hostel, fodder)
A stock of food "for M men for D days" is $M \times D$ man-days of food. After t days the stock left is $M(D - t)$ man-days, to be shared by the new headcount:
$$\text{days left} = \frac{M_1 (D - t)}{M_2}$$
400 men have food for 25 days; after 5 days 100 more men arrive → stock left $= 400 \times 20 = 8000$ man-days ÷ 500 = 16 days. If men leave instead, the headcount drops and the stock lasts longer. If nobody joins or leaves, the remaining days are simply $D - t$.

### Work left after some days / reinforcement mid-work
Convert the whole job into man-days first. 60 men need 40 days → job = 2400 man-days. After 10 days they have done 600, leaving 1800 for the new team. If 10 men leave, the remaining 50 need $\frac{1800}{50} = 36$ days more. Always apply the chain to the **remaining** work, never to the whole job again.

### Men, women and boys (efficiency equivalence)
"3 men or 5 women can do a work in 12 days" pins the unit rates: one man does $\frac{1}{3 \times 12} = \frac{1}{36}$ per day, one woman $\frac{1}{60}$ per day. Any team can then be priced: 6 men + 5 women $= \frac{6}{36} + \frac{5}{60} = \frac14$ per day → 4 days. Read "or" as "the two teams are equally big in work terms".

### Efficiency inside the chain
If one person is twice as efficient, count him as 2 men. A team of 3 men and 2 boys, where a man = 2 boys, is $3 \times 2 + 2 = 8$ boy-units. Converting everyone to one standard unit before multiplying avoids all confusion.

### Common traps
- Writing more men in the numerator (more men → FEWER days).
- Forgetting to subtract the elapsed days from the provisions.
- Applying the chain to the full job instead of the remaining job.
- Counting a man's efficiency twice — E enters the product once.

### Quick revision
- $M_1D_1H_1E_1 = M_2D_2H_2E_2$ for the same work.
- Provisions: stock $= M(D-t)$ man-days ÷ new headcount.
- Mid-work: remaining work = total − (rate × days gone).
- Equivalence: rate of one man = $\frac{1}{\text{men} \times \text{days}}$; price every team this way.
- Sanity: more men / more hours / higher efficiency → fewer days.

Why: the total job is a fixed number of man-hours, so the two products must be equal.

subtopics.title: Joining / Leaving Mid-work, Alternate Days & Wages
subtopics.concept:
Three classic twists, one method — compute the work actually done by each worker:

- **A leaves after t days:** work done $= \frac{t}{T_A}$; the rest is finished by B alone.
- **Alternate days:** pair the days. A 2-day cycle does $\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B}$; count complete cycles, then handle the leftover.
- **Wages:** money splits in the ratio of work actually done — i.e. the ratio of daily rates when all work the full time.

Wage ratio for full-time co-workers: $A : B = \frac{1}{T_A} : \frac{1}{T_B} = T_B : T_A$.

subtopics.notes:
### One method: count the work actually done
Every "twist" question in this family — someone leaves, someone joins late, people work on alternate days, wages are divided — is solved the same way. Put the job in LCM units, write each worker's rate per day, then **add up the work each worker actually did** and set the total equal to the whole job.

### A leaves after t days
A can do the job in $T_A$ days and works only t days: he completes $\frac{t}{T_A}$ of it. The rest, $1 - \frac{t}{T_A}$, is finished by whoever continues — alone or in a team — at their own rate. In units this is even simpler: job 30 units, A does 3/day, works 2 days → 6 units done, 24 left.
A (12 days) works 3 days, B (18 days) finishes alone: A did $\frac14$; B needs $\frac34 \times 18 = 13.5$ days.

### B joins after t days
A works alone first. Add his solo work to the team work: if A starts and B joins after t days,
$$\frac{t}{T_A} + \left(T_{\text{team}} - t\right)\left(\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B}\right) = 1$$
A (20 days) starts; B (15 days) joins after 5 days. A alone did $\frac14$; the pair does $\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{15} = \frac{7}{60}$ per day → $\frac{45}{7}$ days more, about 14.4 total. Read carefully: the question may ask for the total days or the days after joining.

### Alternate days
Pair the days into a **cycle**. Working one day each, starting with A, one 2-day cycle does $\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B}$ of the job. Divide the job by the cycle output to get the number of complete cycles, then walk the leftover days one at a time — **the next day is the other worker's turn**.
A = 8 days (3 units of 24), B = 12 days (2 units): cycle = 5 units per 2 days. Four cycles = 8 days, 20 units done, 4 left. Day 9 is A's: 3 units, 1 left. Day 10 is B's: 2 units/day → half a day. Total $9\frac12$ days. Never assume the leftover finishes inside the cycle pattern — check whose turn day 9 actually is.

### Wages follow work done
The wage is payment for work, so money splits in the ratio of the work each person actually did:
$$w_A : w_B = (\text{rate}_A \times \text{days}_A) : (\text{rate}_B \times \text{days}_B)$$
When everyone works the full time together, the days cancel and the wage ratio is just the **rate ratio**. A alone 10 days, B alone 15, together they earn ₹600: rates 3 : 2 → shares ₹360 and ₹240.
If one worker's time is unknown, first find his rate from the group rate (his rate = team rate − others). A (12 days), B (20 days) and C together finish in 5 days for ₹1200: team rate $\frac15$; C's rate $= \frac15 - \frac{1}{12} - \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1}{15}$; ratio $5:3:4$ → C gets ₹400.

### Reading the question twice
The same numbers support four different questions: how many days in total, how many days after the change, what fraction of work each did, and whose share is what. Mark the words *total*, *more*, *alone* and *remaining* before computing — most lost marks here are reading losses, not arithmetic ones.

### Quick revision
- Work done = rate × days worked; whoever continues inherits the remainder.
- Alternate days: count 2-day cycles, then hand the tail to the correct worker.
- Wages = work done ratio; equal days → rate ratio.
- Unknown member's rate = team rate − sum of known rates.
- Sanity: the stronger worker earns the bigger share.

patterns.name: A leaves after t days
patterns.howToSpot: A works a few days and leaves; B (or B and C, or the rest of the team) completes the remaining work; the remaining or total days are asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Job in units; find A's daily rate.
2. Work done by A in t days = rate × t; subtract from the job.
3. Divide the remainder by the daily rate of whoever continues.

Why: each worker is only paid in work-units — when A stops, his units stop flowing.

example.q: A can do a work in 12 days and B in 18 days. A works for 3 days and then leaves. In how many days will B alone finish the remaining work?
example.solution: A does $\frac{3}{12} = \frac14$. Remaining $= \frac34$ → B needs $\frac34 \times 18 = 13.5$ days.

patterns.name: B joins after t days
patterns.howToSpot: A starts alone; after some days B (or a team) joins and the rest is done together; the total time or the after-joining time is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Work done by A alone = rate × t.
2. Remaining work ÷ combined daily rate = days after joining.
3. Add the solo days for the total time.

Why: the job has two phases with different daily rates; each phase is a rate × time sum.

example.q: A can finish a work in 20 days and B in 15 days. A works alone for 5 days, after which B joins him. In how many days is the whole work finished?
example.solution: A did $\frac14$. Remaining $\frac34$ at $\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{15} = \frac{7}{60}$/day → $\frac{45}{7} = 6\frac37$ days more → about $11\frac37$ total.

patterns.name: Alternate days (A one day, B next)
patterns.howToSpot: 'A and B work on alternate days, A starting' — find the total time, or which day the work ends.
patterns.logic:
1. One 2-day cycle does $\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B}$ of the job (use units).
2. Complete as many full cycles as fit; note the work left.
3. Walk the leftover one day at a time — the next day belongs to the OTHER worker. A partial last day counts as a fraction of a day.

Why: pairing the days turns a jumpy schedule into a smooth repeated cycle.

example.q: A can finish a work in 8 days and B in 12 days. Working on alternate days beginning with A, in how many days is the work finished?
example.solution:
Job 24 units; A 3/day, B 2/day. Cycle = 5 units. 4 cycles (8 days) → 20 done.
Day 9 (A): 3 → 1 left. Day 10 (B): half a day. Total $9\frac12$ days.

patterns.name: Wages split by work done
patterns.howToSpot: A total wage for a joint job is given; find one person's share — sometimes with unequal days worked or an unknown member.
patterns.logic:
1. Write each worker's rate (in units/day) and multiply by his own days.
2. The wage ratio is the ratio of those products.
3. Give each worker his fraction of the total money.

Why: wages pay for work delivered, and work = rate × days.

practice.q: A can finish a work in 6 days and B in 12 days. They work on alternate days, A starting on the first day. The work is completed in:
practice.solution:
Per 2 days: $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the work.
4 cycles (8 days) complete exactly $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ⇒ finished on day 8.

practice.q: 45 men would complete a piece of work in 16 days. They work for 4 days, after which 36 more men join them. The remaining work is now completed in:
practice.solution:
Total work $= 720$ man-days; done in 4 days $= 180$.
Remaining $= 540$ with 81 men ⇒ $\frac{540}{81} = 6\frac{2}{3}$ days.

practice.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 16 hours respectively. Both are opened together for 4 hours; then a drain pipe C, which can empty the full tank in 24 hours, is also opened. The total time taken to fill the tank is:
practice.solution:
In 4 h, A + B fill $\frac{7}{48} \times 4 = \frac{7}{12}$; remaining $= \frac{5}{12}$.
New net rate $= \frac{7}{48} - \frac{1}{24} = \frac{5}{48}$ ⇒ time $= \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{48}{5} = 4$ h.
Total = 4 + 4 = **8 hours**.
practice.shortcut: Stage 1 does 7/12; stage 2 rate 5/48 finishes the rest in exactly 4 h.

practice.q: A is 3 times as fast a worker as B and takes 24 days less than B for the same work. If they work together, the work is completed in:
practice.solution:
Times: $x$ and $3x$ with $3x - x = 24$ ⇒ $x = 12$ (A = 12, B = 36).
Together: $\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{4}{36} = \frac{1}{9}$ ⇒ 9 days.
practice.shortcut: Difference of times = 2 units = 24 ⇒ A 12, B 36; ab/(a+b) = 9.

Tank = 30 units; stage 1: $5 \times 2 = 10$ units done, 20 left.
Stage 2: net $= 5 - 1 = 4$ units/h → 5 more hours. Total $= 2 + 5 = 7$ hours.

practice.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 20 hours respectively. Both are opened together for 4 hours; then B is closed and a drain pipe C, which can empty the full tank in 30 hours, is opened along with A. The total time taken to fill the tank is:
practice.solution:
Tank = 60 units. Stage 1: $(5+3) \times 4 = 32$ units done, 28 left.
Stage 2: net $= 5 - 2 = 3$ units/h → $\frac{28}{3} = 9\frac{1}{3}$ h more. Total $= 13\frac{1}{3}$ hours.

practice.q: If 18 men can complete a piece of work in 25 days, in how many days will 30 men complete the same work?
12 men working 8 hours a day can complete a work in 15 days. In how many days will 18 men working 10 hours a day complete the same work?
A garrison of 400 men has provisions for 25 days. After 5 days, 100 more men join the garrison. The provisions will now last for:
20 men working 9 hours a day complete a piece of work in 24 days. How many men working 8 hours a day will complete it in 15 days?
A fort has provisions for 300 men for 45 days. After 10 days, 100 men leave the fort. For how many more days will the provisions last?
practice.shortcut: Fewer men → the stock lasts longer than the original 35 remaining days.

practice.q: 60 men can complete a piece of work in 40 days. They start together and work for 10 days, after which 10 men leave. In how many days will the remaining work be finished?
practice.solution: Job $= 2400$ man-days; done $= 600$; left $= 1800$ with 50 men → 36 days.

practice.q: If 3 men or 5 women can complete a piece of work in 12 days, then 6 men and 5 women together will complete it in:
8 men or 12 boys can finish a piece of work in 10 days. 8 men and 8 boys together will finish it in:

120 men can complete a piece of work in 60 days. They work together for the first 12 days; after that some men leave, and the remaining men complete the rest of the work in 72 days. How many men left after the 12th day?
practice.solution:
Job $= 7200$ man-days; done $= 1440$; left $= 5760$.
Men needed $= \frac{5760}{72} = 80$ → $120 - 80 = 40$ men must leave.

practice.q: A can do a piece of work in 12 days and B can do it in 18 days. A works for 3 days and then leaves. B alone will finish the remaining work in:
practice.solution: A did $\frac{3}{12} = \frac14$; remaining $= \frac34$. B's time $= \frac34 \times 18 = 13.5$ days.

practice.q: A and B together receive ₹600 for completing a job. A alone can do the job in 10 days and B alone in 15 days. A's share is:
A can complete a work in 20 days and B in 15 days. A works alone for 5 days, after which B joins him. In how many days in total is the work completed?
practice.solution:
A alone did $\frac{5}{20} = \frac14$. Remaining $\frac34$ at $\frac{7}{60}$/day → $\frac{45}{7} = 6\frac37$ days.
Total $= 5 + 6\frac37 = 11\frac37$ days.

practice.q: A can complete a job in 3 days and B in 6 days. They work on alternate days, A starting on day 1. The job is finished in:
practice.solution: Per 2-day cycle: $\frac13 + \frac16 = \frac12$. Two cycles = 4 days complete the job exactly.

practice.q: A can do a work in 10 days, B in 15 days and C in 30 days. All three start together, but A leaves after 2 days. For how many more days will B and C work to finish the job?
practice.solution:
Job = 30 units; rates 3, 2, 1. In 2 days all three did 12 units; 18 left.
B + C = 3 units/day → $18 \div 3 = 6$ days.

practice.q: A can finish a piece of work in 12 days and B in 24 days. A starts the work and B joins him after 6 days. The whole work is finished in:
practice.solution:
A alone: $\frac{6}{12} = \frac12$ done. Remaining $\frac12$ at $\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{24} = \frac18$/day → 4 days.
Total $= 6 + 4 = 10$ days.

practice.q: A, B and C together complete a job for ₹4,500. A alone can do it in 10 days, B in 12 days and C in 15 days. B's share is:
A can finish a work in 8 days and B in 12 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. The work is finished in:
practice.solution:
Job 24 units; A 3/day, B 2/day; cycle = 5 units per 2 days.
4 cycles = 8 days → 20 done. Day 9 (A): 3 → 1 left. Day 10 (B, 2/day): $\frac12$ day.
Total $= 9\frac12$ days.
practice.shortcut: Day 9 belongs to A, not B — the turns alternate every single day.

practice.q: A and B undertake to complete a piece of work for ₹1,200. A can do it in 12 days and B in 20 days. With the help of C, they complete it in 5 days. C's share is:
